title: Commutative diagram with mismatch arrow: do two routes give the same answer?
summary: A commutative diagram asks whether two different routes between the same start and end give the same answer. Here: encode then flow in the latent space versus flow in the true space then encode, with the mismatch written on an arrow.

media.alt: A diagram with five boxes: state x(0) on the left, latent z(0) and state x(T) in the middle, latent z(T) [route 1] and encode(x(T)) [route 2] on the right; teal arrows encode and learned flow along the top, blue dashed arrows true flow and encode along the bottom; a red double arrow between the two right boxes labelled mismatch of 3.2e-3.
media.caption: Reference render of class F6.7 (design-system gallery). The data are synthetic and exist only to demonstrate the form.

source.note: Plot class from the design system's plot taxonomy; synthetic demonstration data.

read_the_figure.question: Do two routes give the same answer?
read_the_figure.axes: No axes. Boxes are objects (states and latent states), arrows are maps (encode, true flow, learned flow). The two routes run left to right and end in the two boxes on the right edge.
look_at: Do the two routes start at the same object and end in the same space?
Which arrows are true (reference) maps and which are learned?
What is the mismatch and in what norm and units is it given?
Is the mismatch relative or absolute, and for which initial state and horizon T?
as_drawn: Route 1 (teal): state x(0), encode to latent z(0), learned flow to latent z(T). Route 2 (blue, dashed): true flow to state x(T), then encode to encode(x(T)).
A red double-headed arrow joins the two end boxes with the label mismatch, norm of dz equal to 3.2e-3.
The note at the top says it is a static diagram with a synthetic value. The mismatch is one number for one start and one horizon.
The diagram does not say which norm is used, whether the mismatch is relative, or what the scale of z(T) is.
read_the_figure.proves: If the mismatch is zero for every start and every horizon, the learned flow is exactly the true flow seen through the encoder. A nonzero value measures, for one start and one horizon, how far the routes disagree.
if_wrong: No mismatch value on the arrow: the diagram is only a statement of intent, not a measurement.
Mismatch given without a norm or a scale: 3.2e-3 could be negligible or huge depending on the size of z.
Both routes use a learned map: the comparison is no longer against a reference.
must_check: mismatch value on arrow: the whole point is a number for the disagreement; a diagram without it cannot be checked.

terms.meaning: A diagram of maps where all routes between the same two objects give the same result.
A map from the state to a latent representation.
The map taking the initial state to the state at time T under the real dynamics.
The map taking a latent state to its value at time T under the learned latent dynamics.
The distance between the end points of the two routes; zero if the diagram commutes.
A bound on how much a map can stretch distances; it controls how errors grow when maps are composed.

remember: The diagram commutes if E(Phi_T(x0)) = Psi_T(E(x0)).
Mismatch = distance between the two end points, in a stated norm.
Relative mismatch = delta / norm of the latent state.
Errors compound: delta_k at most eps (L^k - 1) / (L - 1) with per-step defect eps and Lipschitz constant L.
State the start, the horizon and the norm.

understand.title: Marks and encodings
understand.text: Boxes are objects and arrows are maps; colour and line style separate the learned route (teal) from the reference route (blue dashed). A bold red double-headed arrow joins the two ends, and its label carries the measured value. Position matters only topologically: what matters is which arrows share ends.

understand.title: Why this form answers the question
understand.text: Plain language: if a model is right, it should not matter whether you first translate to the latent space and then evolve, or first evolve and then translate. The diagram turns that sentence into a picture: two paths, one square. The distance between the two path ends is the error in one number. It also shows which parts are learned and which are exact, so you know what is being tested.

understand.title: How it misleads
understand.text: A single number for one initial condition may hide a large variation over the data distribution; the diagram does not show spread. A mismatch of 3e-3 has no meaning without a norm, a scale and a horizon: errors in the latent space and in the original space are not the same. And a small mismatch for the whole route does not locate the error: it may come from the encoder, the decoder or the flow.

understand.title: Alternatives
understand.text: A plot of the mismatch against horizon T (F6.9) shows how errors accumulate. A histogram of the mismatch over many start states shows the distribution. A table breaking the error into encoder error, flow error and decoder error says where to improve.

understand.title: A variant to create
understand.text: Print the mismatch as a percentage of the norm of z(T), add the distribution over 1000 start states as a small histogram beside the arrow, and mark which single arrow contributes the most to the total.

steps.title: What commuting means
steps.note: The two routes of the diagram give the same latent state.

steps.title: The mismatch
steps.note: Zero if the diagram commutes; state the norm and the horizon.

steps.title: Errors that compound
steps.note: Verified by direct summation. If 3.2e-3 were a per-step defect and L = 1.1, ten steps could reach 5.1e-2.

worked.title: Reading the commutative diagram of the reference render
worked.problem: (1) Which two objects are compared and which maps lead to each? (2) What would a zero mismatch mean? (3) If the mismatch of 3.2e-3 were the defect of each of ten successive steps and the learned map has L = 1.1, what bound do you get for the accumulated mismatch?

solution.text: (1) The compared objects are latent z(T) [route 1: encode, then learned flow] and encode(x(T)) [route 2: true flow, then encode]. Both are latent states, so they can be subtracted.
(2) The learned flow would be exactly the true flow seen through the encoder, for this start and horizon.

worked.answer: The two end boxes on the right are compared; zero would mean the diagram commutes; with a per-step defect of 3.2e-3 and L = 1.1 ten steps can reach about 5.1e-2.

analyze.hint: Distribution over starts, horizon, norm and scale.

analyze.q: How would you decide whether the mismatch comes from the encoder or from the learned flow?
analyze.hint: Compare each arrow with a reference separately.

analyze.q: What happens to the bound in step 3 if L is less than 1?

evaluate.q: A mismatch of 3.2e-3 is reported. Is it small?
evaluate.hint: Compared with what? The norm of z, the data noise, the tolerance of the application.

create: Draw the diagram with the mismatch as a relative percentage and a small violin plot over many initial states.
Extend the diagram with a decoder and show the mismatch back in the original coordinates.

checks.q: What does it mean for the diagram to commute?
checks.answer: Going around either route from the same start gives the same end point, so the learned latent dynamics agree with the true dynamics seen through the encoder.

checks.q: |z(T)| = 0.5 and the mismatch is 3.2e-3. What is the relative mismatch?
Why can one mismatch value be misleading?
checks.hint: What is missing from a single number?
checks.answer: It is for one initial state and one horizon in one norm: the distribution over states and the growth with horizon are hidden, and the source of the error (encoder, flow) is not identified.
